routes.description: Establish that the earliest Christian sources report Jesus as raised in bodily continuity, then support the historical credibility of those reports through transmission, attestation, and relevant circumstantial considerations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources can be treated as sufficiently early and historically connected to witnesses, their resurrection language is bodily rather than merely immaterial, and the principal skeptical alternatives do not defeat the resulting inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect credible early-source testimony to the historical conclusion that Jesus rose bodily from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early and multiply attested proclamation of burial, resurrection, and appearances.
Show that spiritual-body and related source language denotes transformed bodily continuity rather than a nonphysical survival claim.
Ground the relevant texts and early church testimony in a historically credible chain connected to apostolic witnesses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the claimed event from proposed pagan dying-and-rising parallels in chronology, content, and documentary support.
Explain how conversion, persecution, martyrdom traditions, and early expansion bear on the sincerity and claimed witness basis of the proclamation.

routes.description: Withhold the historical conclusion of bodily resurrection by applying inductive historical standards, challenging the sources' provenance and bodily meaning, and supplying analogues or ordinary explanations for the cited evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative evidence does not overcome the event's weak experiential analogy, the sources remain materially uncertain or internally disputed, or the supporting phenomena are adequately compatible with non-resurrection explanations.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available early Christian claims do not warrant concluding historically that Jesus bodily rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Require inductive and revisable historical inference while distinguishing divine possibility from evidence that this event occurred.
Challenge the provenance, coherence, and physical interpretation of the New Testament and patristic source base.
Place resurrection claims alongside ancient religious analogues and ordinary mechanisms capable of explaining belief formation and transmission.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether apostolic succession, named witnesses, and martyrdom traditions are independently verifiable rather than dependent on later institutional claims.
Separate sincere costly commitment and movement growth from the factual correctness of the resurrection proclamation.

sections.title: Historical Method, Miracle Possibility, and Evidential Burden
sections.rationale: This issue determines what kind of inference ancient testimony can support, how present experience and historical analogy constrain that inference, and why divine capability alone does or does not establish the reported event.

sections.title: Earliest Resurrection Sources and the Meaning of Bodily
sections.rationale: The motion turns directly on whether Paul and other early Christian texts proclaim bodily continuity, a transformed physical body, or a spiritual event that conflicts with later flesh-and-bones presentations.

sections.title: Source Provenance, Apostolic Transmission, and Multiple Attestation
sections.rationale: The historical force of the resurrection reports depends on authorship, authenticity, chronology, witness connection, cross-community transmission, and whether apparent convergence supplies independent attestation.

sections.title: Pagan Resurrection Parallels and Comparative Context
sections.rationale: Proposed Attis, Osiris, Baal, and related parallels bear on the use of historical analogy, the claimed uniqueness of the Christian account, and competing explanations of the narrative's religious context.

sections.title: Martyrdom, Conversion, and Early Christian Growth
sections.rationale: Costly commitment, apostolic martyrdom traditions, Paul's conversion, and movement expansion may support witness-based sincerity, while alternative social explanations test whether those facts establish more than belief.
